# 6. ENTITY AUTHORITY AND SINGLE-PURPOSE ENTITY ISSUES

**6.1 Execution authority — the 75% member approval requirement (critical).**

**Facts.** The Operating Agreement vests the Managing Member with authority to execute "loan documents, promissory notes, deeds of trust, mortgages, security agreements, guaranties, and related instruments" (§3.1(e)), but §3.2 makes "any financing or refinancing of the Property in an amount in excess of $1,000,000" a "Major Decision" requiring the prior written approval of Members holding at least **seventy-five percent (75%)** of the outstanding membership interests. GDG holds **72%**; Tidewater 18%; Harborline 10%. The Operating Agreement summary expressly notes that "GDG alone cannot approve any Major Decision."

**Consequence.** A $14,750,000 mortgage is a Major Decision. GDG's signature — and therefore Mr. Graydon's signature as sole member and manager of GDG — is **not** sufficient authority to bind Borrower. At least one Passive Member must join (GDG plus Tidewater = 90%; GDG plus Harborline = 82%). Title Requirement 8(b) and 8(c) require satisfactory evidence of the authority of the persons executing the Mortgage and of GDG, and the title company will read the Operating Agreement. The legal opinion required by Term Sheet §12.1(h)(ii) (due authorisation) cannot be given without it.

**Draft.** Section 5.1 of the Draft Mortgage contains an affirmative representation, in terms, that execution has been authorised by Members holding not less than 75% under Operating Agreement §3.2(ii). That representation must be true at signing. **Action (before execution):** obtain a written consent or resolution signed by GDG and at least one Passive Member (recommend all three, which also supports the Operating Agreement Amendment — see §6.2), certified as true and complete, together with the incumbency certificates.

**6.2 Single-purpose entity provisions are absent and must be papered (critical).**

**Facts — what the Operating Agreement does contain and what it does not.**

| Requirement | Position under the Operating Agreement | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Independent manager with bankruptcy consent | No provision; "does not impose any requirement for GDG to appoint or maintain an independent director, independent manager, or springing member" (§3.1) | GDG (i.e. Mr. Graydon) can file Borrower into bankruptcy unilaterally |
| Bankruptcy filing as a Major Decision | The Major Decisions list (§3.2) omits bankruptcy, insolvency or reorganisation | No supermajority or third-party consent required |
| Separateness covenants | None; no prohibition on commingling, no requirement of separate accounts or records, no arms'-length requirement | Substantive consolidation risk destroys the non-recourse structure |
| Single-purpose purpose clause | Purpose is "…to acquire, own, hold, manage, lease, renovate, improve, operate, finance, refinance, and ultimately dispose of" the Property "and to engage in any and all activities necessary, incidental, or related thereto" (§1.4) | The catch-all is broad; the agreement "does not contain any language restricting the Company to single-purpose entity status" |
| Lender consent to dissolution | No provision; dissolution on 75% member consent or sale of the Property (§8.1) | Borrower can dissolve without Lender consent |
| Amendment of SPE provisions | Amendments require 75% member consent, plus each affected Member for changes to economic rights or capital obligations (§9.1); no lender consent requirement | SPE protections could be removed without Lender's knowledge |
| Change of control | No provision capturing indirect or upstream changes; §4.1 applies only to transfers of membership interests in Borrower (§4.2, note following) | See §6.4 below |

**One correction to your notes.** Your markup describes the purpose clause as allowing "any lawful business." The Operating Agreement summary actually quotes a property-specific purpose clause with a broad incidental-activities catch-all (§1.4). The difference matters because the representation we draft must match the document: the Draft Mortgage's §7.6(b)(iii) requires an amended purpose clause restricting the business to the Property and incidental activities, and §5.10 makes the representation by reference to the Operating Agreement **as amended by the Operating Agreement Amendment**. I have deliberately not drafted a representation that the current agreement already complies, because it does not (see next paragraph).

**Draft treatment.** You asked that the SPE covenants be drafted as though the Operating Agreement already complies, with separate representations. I have taken a slightly different approach, for one reason: a representation that the organisational documents contain compliant SPE provisions would be knowingly false as of today, is an Event of Default and a recourse carve-out on day one, and would give the borrower's counsel an argument that we drafted around a known fact. Instead:

> (a) Section 6.12 contains the full separateness and single-purpose covenant package, binding Borrower directly under the Mortgage (so it binds regardless of what the Operating Agreement says), including the Independent Manager approval requirement for bankruptcy filings, dissolution, merger or consolidation (§6.12(k));
>
> (b) Section 7.6 defines the **Operating Agreement Amendment**, requires it to be executed by all three Members and effective not later than the Closing Date, specifies its contents (independent manager, separateness, single-purpose purpose clause, unanimity plus Lender consent for amendment of those provisions), and prohibits any amendment, modification or waiver of any single-purpose entity provision without Lender's consent in each instance (§7.6(a)–(b));
>
> (c) Section 5.10 makes the representation that the organisational documents, **as amended by the Operating Agreement Amendment**, contain the required provisions, and that the amendment has been adopted; and
>
> (d) Section 7.6(b) contains an express acknowledgment that the Operating Agreement did not contain these provisions as of the Term Sheet date, so that the record is honest and the amendment is a documented closing condition rather than a fiction.

**Action (before closing):** (i) circulate a form of Operating Agreement Amendment for Borrower's counsel (Cartwright & Lyons LLP); (ii) confirm that the 75% amendment threshold in §9.1 is sufficient — I read the SPE amendments as not altering economic rights or increasing capital obligations, so the §9.1 proviso requiring each affected Member's consent should not be triggered, but all three Members should sign in any event, which removes the question; (iii) confirm that Borrower's Articles of Organization and any registered-agent filings do not need conforming amendments.

**6.3 Member consents and general partner authority.**

> **(a) Tidewater.** Tidewater Opportunity Fund II LP is a Delaware limited partnership whose general partner is Tidewater GP Holdings LLC, which "has the exclusive authority to manage and direct the affairs of Tidewater" (Operating Agreement §2.1). The limited partnership agreement is not in the record. Obtain either the relevant provisions of the LPA authorising the execution of the Operating Agreement Amendment and member consents, or a GP authorisation certificate/resolution. Term Sheet §12.1(g) requires Borrower's organisational documents but does not expressly pick up Member-level authority; add it to the closing checklist.
>
> **(b) Harborline.** Harborline Capital Advisors LLC is a Delaware LLC whose "members and managers … have not been disclosed in this summary" (Operating Agreement §2.1). Obtain its organisational documents, good standing certificate and incumbency certificate.
>
> **(c) GDG.** Mr. Graydon is GDG's sole member and manager and "exercises sole and exclusive control over GDG" (Operating Agreement §2.1). A certificate of GDG is sufficient.

**6.4 Indirect transfers and change of control (your item 4).** The Operating Agreement restricts only transfers of membership interests in Borrower (§4.1), and expressly does not "restrict or address changes in the internal or upstream ownership, management, or control of any Member entity." The summary gives three illustrations: Mr. Graydon could sell his interest in GDG (the 72% Managing Member) without triggering the transfer restrictions; Tidewater's GP could itself be acquired; and Harborline's internal ownership could change entirely. Worse, §4.2(c) permits Tidewater's GP to direct transfers of Tidewater's 18% interest to "any successor fund managed by Tidewater GP Holdings LLC or any Affiliate thereof" — an undefined term — without any other Member's consent.

**Draft.** Section 7.3 of the Draft Mortgage has three limbs: (a) transfers of the Property; (b) direct transfers of interests in Borrower exceeding 10% individually or 25% in the aggregate, with the Term Sheet's carve-out for transfers among existing Members (subject to notice, a written confirmation that the transferee is bound by the single-purpose entity covenants, and compliance with the Operating Agreement); and (c) **any change in Control of Borrower, GDG, Guarantor or any other Person that Controls Borrower**, by whatever means, including replacement or resignation of the Independent Manager. Limb (c) is an addition beyond Term Sheet §10.3, which addresses only direct transfers of interests in Borrower; it is flagged in Section 10 below for the Bank's approval. Note also a conflict we should resolve in the Operating Agreement Amendment: Term Sheet §10.3 permits transfers "among the existing members of Borrower" without consent, while Operating Agreement §4.1 requires consent of the Managing Member and 75% of the Members for any transfer — the lender's covenant cannot authorise what the operating agreement prohibits, so the amendment should align them.

**6.5 Documentary inconsistencies requiring correction.**

> **(a) Registered agent.** Term Sheet §1.2 names "Capitol Registered Agents Inc." at 1201 Main Street, Suite 410, Columbia; Operating Agreement §1.3 names "Statehouse Registered Agents, Inc." at the same address. One is wrong. Because the Mortgage is recorded and may be served by substituted service, and because the certificate of good standing must match the registered agent of record, resolve before closing. The Draft Mortgage does not recite the registered agent (it is not a required recital), which avoids perpetuating the error in the instrument.
>
> **(b) Audited financial statements.** Term Sheet §7.3(a) requires annual **audited** financial statements of Borrower within 120 days of fiscal year end. Operating Agreement §6.2 requires only **reviewed** statements. The Draft Mortgage implements the Term Sheet (§12.3(a)) and expressly notes the inconsistency and Borrower's obligation to comply (§12.3, final paragraph). Practical point: Borrower was formed on January 12, 2024, so its first audited fiscal year will be 2025, due by April 30, 2026. Consider whether the Bank wants a reviewed stub for FY2024 and a covenant that accommodates the first audit cycle.
>
> **(c) Borrower's fiscal year and reporting.** Calendar year (Operating Agreement §6.3). The reporting dates in the Draft Mortgage are drafted to the fiscal year end accordingly.

# 7. LOAN TERMS REQUIRING PRECISION

**7.1 Yield maintenance (your item 5).**

**What the Term Sheet says.** Section 4.2 provides for prepayment in whole (not in part) in months 25–48 on 30 days' notice, with a premium equal to the **greater of** (a) 1.00% of the outstanding principal balance, or (b) the present value of the excess of (i) interest that would have accrued on the prepaid principal at the Note rate for the period from prepayment through the end of the 48th month, over (ii) interest that would accrue at "the treasury rate plus fifty (50) basis points" for that period, "discounted to present value at the treasury rate."

**What your notes propose.** A formula in which the premium equals the positive excess of the present value of all remaining scheduled payments of principal and interest (discounted at the Treasury Rate) over the outstanding principal prepaid, "in no event less than zero."

**Why I did not adopt the formulation in your notes as drafted.** It departs from the executed Term Sheet in three respects, each of which favours the borrower:

> (i) it omits the **1.00% floor**, which the Term Sheet makes part of a "greater of" test — under your formula a premium of zero is possible;
>
> (ii) it computes the differential by reference to the **Note rate stream discounted at the Treasury Rate** and subtracts principal, rather than computing the **interest differential between the Note rate and the Treasury Rate plus 50 basis points**; the two approaches produce materially different numbers when the curve is steep, and the Term Sheet's construct is the bargained-for one; and
>
> (iii) it leaves the "treasury rate + 50 bps" ambiguity unresolved, whereas the Term Sheet uses the spread in the comparison stream.

**What the Draft Mortgage does.** Section 13.2 implements the Term Sheet's "greater of" structure: (a) 1.00% of the principal prepaid; or (b) the present value, discounted at the Treasury Rate, of the excess of interest at the Note rate (after the SOFR floor) over interest at the Treasury Rate plus 50 basis points, for the period from prepayment to the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period, with monthly discounting, a proration convention for a mid-month prepayment, a floor of zero on the computed excess (the floor operates through the 1.00% minimum in clause (a), so the premium can never be less than 1.00%), and a conclusive-calculation clause. "Treasury Rate" is defined in Section 1.1(qq) as the H.15 yield, determined as of the second Business Day preceding prepayment, on the security maturing closest to but not exceeding the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period, with linear interpolation if there is no exact match. The Yield Maintenance Period is defined as ending April 15, 2029 (month 48).

**This resolves your four questions** as follows: (a) CMT, matched to the end of the Yield Maintenance Period, interpolated; (b) discount rate is the Treasury Rate alone, and the 50 basis points is applied to the comparison stream; (c) the premium is the greater of the 1% floor and the computed amount; (d) the computed amount floors at zero but the 1% floor applies regardless. **Two items still need the client:** first, confirm the interpretation of the 50 basis points (we apply it in the comparison stream, consistent with the Term Sheet's text, rather than adding it to the Note rate as you suggested as an alternative reading); second, confirm whether the Bank wants a different interpolation convention (e.g. matched to the remaining loan term rather than to the end of the Yield Maintenance Period). **Enforceability:** the formula is deterministic and objectively calculable, which is the protection against a penalty characterisation; I have also avoided any subjective inputs.

**7.2 Prepayment during the lockout period — a gap in the Term Sheet.** Term Sheet §4.1 prohibits prepayment during months 1–24 and then says "any prepayment made in violation of this restriction shall be subject to a prepayment premium as described in Section 4.2." But §4.2's premium is defined only for prepayments made *during months 25–48*; there is no defined premium for a lockout-period prepayment. Section 13.1 of the Draft Mortgage resolves this by (a) making the prohibition absolute and permitting Lender to refuse any tender, and (b) providing that if Lender elects to accept a tender, the Yield Maintenance Premium is computed as though the prepayment had been made on the first day of the Yield Maintenance Period, plus all other amounts due. That is a drafting solution to an ambiguity, and it should be confirmed. Also confirm that a voluntary prepayment during the lockout period is intended to be an Event of Default (the Draft Mortgage does not make it one; it treats the tender as refusable and, if accepted, premium-bearing).

**7.3 Casualty and condemnation.** The Term Sheet is silent on (a) the thresholds above which the Bank controls insurance proceeds, (b) whether proceeds are applied to the Loan or released for restoration, and (c) whether any prepayment premium applies to an involuntary prepayment. You asked me to confirm the casualty/condemnation carve-out with the client. The Draft Mortgage (Article 15) provides: Lender participation in adjusting claims over $250,000; Borrower restoration permitted where the loss is under $500,000, no default exists and proceeds are sufficient; otherwise Lender's election between restoration (on conditions) and application to the Loan; application **at par** with no premium, penalty or yield maintenance (§13.5, §15.5); and coordination with the LUR where restoration affects the Bay 1 slab (§15.4(d)). The $250,000/$500,000/12-month thresholds are our proposed figures, not deal terms (Section 10). Confirm with Marcus: (i) whether the Bank wants a premium on involuntary prepayments (you noted this is the minority position), and (ii) the thresholds.

**7.4 The DSCR test date — a three-way conflict.**

| Source | First test | Mechanics |
|---|---|---|
| Term Sheet §7.1 | The first full calendar quarter ending after the 24th month — i.e. the quarter ending June 30, 2027, tested by July 15, 2027 | Then quarterly |
| Your markup notes §6 (Financial Covenants) | "first test date April 15, 2027" | — |
| Rent Roll, Summary tab ("DSCR Covenant Testing Commencement") | "April 15, 2027 (Month 24 post-closing)" | — |

The Term Sheet is the controlling document and is internally coherent: a quarterly test measured on trailing twelve-month NOI must be measured at a quarter end, and April 15, 2027 is not a quarter end. The Draft Mortgage follows the Term Sheet (Section 12.1(a): the calendar quarter ending June 30, 2027, and quarterly thereafter) and defines Net Operating Income and Annual Debt Service on a trailing-twelve-month and forward-looking basis respectively (Section 1.1(bb), (b)). Flag: the first test will measure a trailing twelve-month period ending June 30, 2027, of which the first two and a half months are within the interest-only period and the last three within amortisation — the definition of Annual Debt Service therefore drives the result. The Draft Mortgage uses the forward-looking definition (25-year amortisation at the then-current rate), which is the more conservative formulation. Confirm with Marcus both the test date and the definition, because together they determine whether the covenant is measured at 0.55x or 0.72x.

**7.5 Net worth and liquidity — whose covenant?** Term Sheet §7.2 states that "**Borrower** shall maintain … a net worth of not less than $1,000,000 … and liquid assets … of not less than $500,000," tested annually under §7.3. Your notes describe these as Guarantor covenants. The Draft Mortgage implements the Term Sheet text as a Borrower covenant (§12.2(a)) and adds the equivalent covenant at the Guarantor level (§12.2(b)), which is what your notes assumed and is the commercially meaningful test — a $1,000,000 net worth covenant measured against a borrower that owns an $18,200,000 property is not a constraint. Section 12.2(b) is an addition (Section 10). Confirm with Marcus whether the Bank wants: (i) the Term Sheet formulation only; (ii) both levels; or (iii) a Guarantor covenant at a materially higher threshold (Guarantor's stated net worth is approximately $28,000,000 per Term Sheet §1.3, although no personal financial statement is in the file).

**7.6 Default mechanics — two gaps and one sequencing problem.**

> **(a) Late charge versus payment default.** Term Sheet §3.11 assesses a 5% late charge on any monthly installment not received within ten **calendar** days of the due date; Term Sheet §11.2(a) gives a cure period of five **business** days for payment defaults. The default therefore occurs before the late charge is triggered. The Draft Mortgage preserves both mechanisms independently: the late charge accrues under §2.6 whether or not a default has occurred and whether or not notice has been given, and the payment default arises under §14.2(a) after five business days, expressly without affecting the late charge or default interest. This is the correct commercial result but should be confirmed as intentional.
>
> **(b) Insurance defaults have no cure period.** Term Sheet §11.1(f) makes a failure to maintain insurance an Event of Default. Term Sheet §11.2(b) excludes "insurance defaults" from the 30-day non-monetary cure period, and §11.2(c) gives no cure period only for SPE and transfer defaults. The result is a gap: insurance defaults fall outside every stated cure category. The Draft Mortgage supplies a ten-day cure period after written notice (§14.2(d)) — a drafting solution, flagged in Section 10.
>
> **(c) Land use restriction defaults.** Neither the Term Sheet nor the commitment specifies the cure mechanics for an LUR breach. The Draft Mortgage provides ten business days after notice, and immediate default where SCDHEC has issued a notice of violation or order or the breach is not curable (§14.2(e)). This implements Title Closer's Note 1 while preserving a short cure window.

**7.7 Interest computation — three terms the Term Sheet leaves open.** The Term Sheet defines "Daily SOFR" (rate published on the applicable business day, or the preceding business day if not published) and imposes a 3.00% floor, but says nothing about (i) the day-count convention, (ii) whether interest for a monthly period is computed on the Daily SOFR in effect on a single day or compounded daily in arrears, or (iii) any requirement for an interest rate cap. Section 2.2 of the Draft Mortgage adopts **actual/360**, a monthly period rate based on Daily SOFR as determined for the applicable Business Day, and no cap requirement. Actual/360 rather than actual/365 adds approximately 1.4% to the effective annual yield on a 5.85% rate. Because the Loan cannot service at the floor rate (Section 4.1), the floating-rate exposure is material: each 100 basis point increase raises annual interest by $147,500, and the term sheet contains no cap, no cap purchase covenant and no rate-lock alternative. **Recommendation:** confirm the day count and compounding convention with Marcus (and conform the Note and the borrower disclosure), and consider requiring a capped or hedged rate at least until the DSCR test date.

**7.8 Guaranty set and characterisation.**

**Facts.** Term Sheet §5.5 is headed "Guaranty" and opens by describing a "**full recourse personal guaranty**," then describes (a) a non-recourse carve-out guaranty, (b) a completion guaranty, and (c) a payment guaranty limited to interest shortfalls during the first fourteen months. Term Sheet §14.3(e) lists a single "Guaranty Agreement" among the closing documents, and §5.4 requires a separate Environmental Indemnity Agreement executed by Borrower and Guarantor.

**Issues.** (i) The "full recourse" description is inconsistent with the non-recourse structure in §5.5(a) and with the limitation of liability the Bank's own structure implies; (ii) the document list does not match the number of guaranties described; (iii) the Interest Shortfall Guaranty's fourteen-month period ends June 15, 2026, exactly the Substantial Completion Deadline, and there is then no credit support between June 2026 and the first DSCR test at the end of June 2027 — the precise period in which the Vacancy Schedule projects the greatest shortfall.

**Draft.** Article 16 treats the Guaranty as three instruments plus the Environmental Indemnity Agreement, cross-references each by name, limits Borrower's and the Members' liability to the Collateral except for the carve-outs (§16.2), sets out the Carve-Out Events (§16.3), preserves the full recourse character of the environmental obligations (§16.4), and describes the Interest Shortfall Guaranty's scope without reducing Borrower's payment obligations (§16.6). The Draft Mortgage does **not** characterise the Guaranty as a full repayment guaranty, because on the Term Sheet's terms it is not. **Action:** confirm with Marcus whether the Bank intends one combined Guaranty Agreement or three separate instruments, and conform the closing checklist and the §14.3 document list. Consider also extending the Interest Shortfall Guaranty to the first DSCR test date.
MDEOF

# 6. ENTITY AUTHORITY AND SINGLE-PURPOSE ENTITY ISSUES

**6.1 Execution authority — the 75% member approval requirement (critical).**

**Facts.** The Operating Agreement vests the Managing Member with authority to execute "loan documents, promissory notes, deeds of trust, mortgages, security agreements, guaranties, and related instruments" (§3.1(e)), but §3.2 makes "any financing or refinancing of the Property in an amount in excess of $1,000,000" a "Major Decision" requiring the prior written approval of Members holding at least **seventy-five percent (75%)** of the outstanding membership interests. GDG holds **72%**; Tidewater 18%; Harborline 10%. The Operating Agreement summary expressly notes that "GDG alone cannot approve any Major Decision."

**Consequence.** A $14,750,000 mortgage is a Major Decision. GDG's signature — and therefore Mr. Graydon's signature as sole member and manager of GDG — is **not** sufficient authority to bind Borrower. At least one Passive Member must join (GDG plus Tidewater = 90%; GDG plus Harborline = 82%). Title Requirement 8(b) and 8(c) require satisfactory evidence of the authority of the persons executing the Mortgage and of GDG, and the title company will read the Operating Agreement. The legal opinion required by Term Sheet §12.1(h)(ii) (due authorisation) cannot be given without it.

**Draft.** Section 5.1 of the Draft Mortgage contains an affirmative representation, in terms, that execution has been authorised by Members holding not less than 75% under Operating Agreement §3.2(ii). That representation must be true at signing. **Action (before execution):** obtain a written consent or resolution signed by GDG and at least one Passive Member (recommend all three, which also supports the Operating Agreement Amendment — see §6.2), certified as true and complete, together with the incumbency certificates.

**6.2 Single-purpose entity provisions are absent and must be papered (critical).**

**Facts — what the Operating Agreement does contain and what it does not.**

| Requirement | Position under the Operating Agreement | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Independent manager with bankruptcy consent | No provision; "does not impose any requirement for GDG to appoint or maintain an independent director, independent manager, or springing member" (§3.1) | GDG (i.e. Mr. Graydon) can file Borrower into bankruptcy unilaterally |
| Bankruptcy filing as a Major Decision | The Major Decisions list (§3.2) omits bankruptcy, insolvency or reorganisation | No supermajority or third-party consent required |
| Separateness covenants | None; no prohibition on commingling, no requirement of separate accounts or records, no arms'-length requirement | Substantive consolidation risk destroys the non-recourse structure |
| Single-purpose purpose clause | Purpose is "…to acquire, own, hold, manage, lease, renovate, improve, operate, finance, refinance, and ultimately dispose of" the Property "and to engage in any and all activities necessary, incidental, or related thereto" (§1.4) | The catch-all is broad; the agreement "does not contain any language restricting the Company to single-purpose entity status" |
| Lender consent to dissolution | No provision; dissolution on 75% member consent or sale of the Property (§8.1) | Borrower can dissolve without Lender consent |
| Amendment of SPE provisions | Amendments require 75% member consent, plus each affected Member for changes to economic rights or capital obligations (§9.1); no lender consent requirement | SPE protections could be removed without Lender's knowledge |
| Change of control | No provision capturing indirect or upstream changes; §4.1 applies only to transfers of membership interests in Borrower (§4.2, note following) | See §6.4 below |

**One correction to your notes.** Your markup describes the purpose clause as allowing "any lawful business." The Operating Agreement summary actually quotes a property-specific purpose clause with a broad incidental-activities catch-all (§1.4). The difference matters because the representation we draft must match the document: the Draft Mortgage's §7.6(b)(iii) requires an amended purpose clause restricting the business to the Property and incidental activities, and §5.10 makes the representation by reference to the Operating Agreement **as amended by the Operating Agreement Amendment**. I have deliberately not drafted a representation that the current agreement already complies, because it does not (see next paragraph).

**Draft treatment.** You asked that the SPE covenants be drafted as though the Operating Agreement already complies, with separate representations. I have taken a slightly different approach, for one reason: a representation that the organisational documents contain compliant SPE provisions would be knowingly false as of today, is an Event of Default and a recourse carve-out on day one, and would give the borrower's counsel an argument that we drafted around a known fact. Instead:

> (a) Section 6.12 contains the full separateness and single-purpose covenant package, binding Borrower directly under the Mortgage (so it binds regardless of what the Operating Agreement says), including the Independent Manager approval requirement for bankruptcy filings, dissolution, merger or consolidation (§6.12(k));
>
> (b) Section 7.6 defines the **Operating Agreement Amendment**, requires it to be executed by all three Members and effective not later than the Closing Date, specifies its contents (independent manager, separateness, single-purpose purpose clause, unanimity plus Lender consent for amendment of those provisions), and prohibits any amendment, modification or waiver of any single-purpose entity provision without Lender's consent in each instance (§7.6(a)–(b));
>
> (c) Section 5.10 makes the representation that the organisational documents, **as amended by the Operating Agreement Amendment**, contain the required provisions, and that the amendment has been adopted; and
>
> (d) Section 7.6(b) contains an express acknowledgment that the Operating Agreement did not contain these provisions as of the Term Sheet date, so that the record is honest and the amendment is a documented closing condition rather than a fiction.

**Action (before closing):** (i) circulate a form of Operating Agreement Amendment for Borrower's counsel (Cartwright & Lyons LLP); (ii) confirm that the 75% amendment threshold in §9.1 is sufficient — I read the SPE amendments as not altering economic rights or increasing capital obligations, so the §9.1 proviso requiring each affected Member's consent should not be triggered, but all three Members should sign in any event, which removes the question; (iii) confirm that Borrower's Articles of Organization and any registered-agent filings do not need conforming amendments.

**6.3 Member consents and general partner authority.**

> **(a) Tidewater.** Tidewater Opportunity Fund II LP is a Delaware limited partnership whose general partner is Tidewater GP Holdings LLC, which "has the exclusive authority to manage and direct the affairs of Tidewater" (Operating Agreement §2.1). The limited partnership agreement is not in the record. Obtain either the relevant provisions of the LPA authorising the execution of the Operating Agreement Amendment and member consents, or a GP authorisation certificate/resolution. Term Sheet §12.1(g) requires Borrower's organisational documents but does not expressly pick up Member-level authority; add it to the closing checklist.
>
> **(b) Harborline.** Harborline Capital Advisors LLC is a Delaware LLC whose "members and managers … have not been disclosed in this summary" (Operating Agreement §2.1). Obtain its organisational documents, good standing certificate and incumbency certificate.
>
> **(c) GDG.** Mr. Graydon is GDG's sole member and manager and "exercises sole and exclusive control over GDG" (Operating Agreement §2.1). A certificate of GDG is sufficient.

**6.4 Indirect transfers and change of control (your item 4).** The Operating Agreement restricts only transfers of membership interests in Borrower (§4.1), and expressly does not "restrict or address changes in the internal or upstream ownership, management, or control of any Member entity." The summary gives three illustrations: Mr. Graydon could sell his interest in GDG (the 72% Managing Member) without triggering the transfer restrictions; Tidewater's GP could itself be acquired; and Harborline's internal ownership could change entirely. Worse, §4.2(c) permits Tidewater's GP to direct transfers of Tidewater's 18% interest to "any successor fund managed by Tidewater GP Holdings LLC or any Affiliate thereof" — an undefined term — without any other Member's consent.

**Draft.** Section 7.3 of the Draft Mortgage has three limbs: (a) transfers of the Property; (b) direct transfers of interests in Borrower exceeding 10% individually or 25% in the aggregate, with the Term Sheet's carve-out for transfers among existing Members (subject to notice, a written confirmation that the transferee is bound by the single-purpose entity covenants, and compliance with the Operating Agreement); and (c) **any change in Control of Borrower, GDG, Guarantor or any other Person that Controls Borrower**, by whatever means, including replacement or resignation of the Independent Manager. Limb (c) is an addition beyond Term Sheet §10.3, which addresses only direct transfers of interests in Borrower; it is flagged in Section 10 below for the Bank's approval. Note also a conflict we should resolve in the Operating Agreement Amendment: Term Sheet §10.3 permits transfers "among the existing members of Borrower" without consent, while Operating Agreement §4.1 requires consent of the Managing Member and 75% of the Members for any transfer — the lender's covenant cannot authorise what the operating agreement prohibits, so the amendment should align them.

**6.5 Documentary inconsistencies requiring correction.**

> **(a) Registered agent.** Term Sheet §1.2 names "Capitol Registered Agents Inc." at 1201 Main Street, Suite 410, Columbia; Operating Agreement §1.3 names "Statehouse Registered Agents, Inc." at the same address. One is wrong. Because the Mortgage is recorded and may be served by substituted service, and because the certificate of good standing must match the registered agent of record, resolve before closing. The Draft Mortgage does not recite the registered agent (it is not a required recital), which avoids perpetuating the error in the instrument.
>
> **(b) Audited financial statements.** Term Sheet §7.3(a) requires annual **audited** financial statements of Borrower within 120 days of fiscal year end. Operating Agreement §6.2 requires only **reviewed** statements. The Draft Mortgage implements the Term Sheet (§12.3(a)) and expressly notes the inconsistency and Borrower's obligation to comply (§12.3, final paragraph). Practical point: Borrower was formed on January 12, 2024, so its first audited fiscal year will be 2025, due by April 30, 2026. Consider whether the Bank wants a reviewed stub for FY2024 and a covenant that accommodates the first audit cycle.
>
> **(c) Borrower's fiscal year and reporting.** Calendar year (Operating Agreement §6.3). The reporting dates in the Draft Mortgage are drafted to the fiscal year end accordingly.

# 7. LOAN TERMS REQUIRING PRECISION

**7.1 Yield maintenance (your item 5).**

**What the Term Sheet says.** Section 4.2 provides for prepayment in whole (not in part) in months 25–48 on 30 days' notice, with a premium equal to the **greater of** (a) 1.00% of the outstanding principal balance, or (b) the present value of the excess of (i) interest that would have accrued on the prepaid principal at the Note rate for the period from prepayment through the end of the 48th month, over (ii) interest that would accrue at "the treasury rate plus fifty (50) basis points" for that period, "discounted to present value at the treasury rate."

**What your notes propose.** A formula in which the premium equals the positive excess of the present value of all remaining scheduled payments of principal and interest (discounted at the Treasury Rate) over the outstanding principal prepaid, "in no event less than zero."

**Why I did not adopt the formulation in your notes as drafted.** It departs from the executed Term Sheet in three respects, each of which favours the borrower:

> (i) it omits the **1.00% floor**, which the Term Sheet makes part of a "greater of" test — under your formula a premium of zero is possible;
>
> (ii) it computes the differential by reference to the **Note rate stream discounted at the Treasury Rate** and subtracts principal, rather than computing the **interest differential between the Note rate and the Treasury Rate plus 50 basis points**; the two approaches produce materially different numbers when the curve is steep, and the Term Sheet's construct is the bargained-for one; and
>
> (iii) it leaves the "treasury rate + 50 bps" ambiguity unresolved, whereas the Term Sheet uses the spread in the comparison stream.

**What the Draft Mortgage does.** Section 13.2 implements the Term Sheet's "greater of" structure: (a) 1.00% of the principal prepaid; or (b) the present value, discounted at the Treasury Rate, of the excess of interest at the Note rate (after the SOFR floor) over interest at the Treasury Rate plus 50 basis points, for the period from prepayment to the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period, with monthly discounting, a proration convention for a mid-month prepayment, a floor of zero on the computed excess (the floor operates through the 1.00% minimum in clause (a), so the premium can never be less than 1.00%), and a conclusive-calculation clause. "Treasury Rate" is defined in Section 1.1(qq) as the H.15 yield, determined as of the second Business Day preceding prepayment, on the security maturing closest to but not exceeding the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period, with linear interpolation if there is no exact match. The Yield Maintenance Period is defined as ending April 15, 2029 (month 48).

**This resolves your four questions** as follows: (a) CMT, matched to the end of the Yield Maintenance Period, interpolated; (b) discount rate is the Treasury Rate alone, and the 50 basis points is applied to the comparison stream; (c) the premium is the greater of the 1% floor and the computed amount; (d) the computed amount floors at zero but the 1% floor applies regardless. **Two items still need the client:** first, confirm the interpretation of the 50 basis points (we apply it in the comparison stream, consistent with the Term Sheet's text, rather than adding it to the Note rate as you suggested as an alternative reading); second, confirm whether the Bank wants a different interpolation convention (e.g. matched to the remaining loan term rather than to the end of the Yield Maintenance Period). **Enforceability:** the formula is deterministic and objectively calculable, which is the protection against a penalty characterisation; I have also avoided any subjective inputs.

**7.2 Prepayment during the lockout period — a gap in the Term Sheet.** Term Sheet §4.1 prohibits prepayment during months 1–24 and then says "any prepayment made in violation of this restriction shall be subject to a prepayment premium as described in Section 4.2." But §4.2's premium is defined only for prepayments made *during months 25–48*; there is no defined premium for a lockout-period prepayment. Section 13.1 of the Draft Mortgage resolves this by (a) making the prohibition absolute and permitting Lender to refuse any tender, and (b) providing that if Lender elects to accept a tender, the Yield Maintenance Premium is computed as though the prepayment had been made on the first day of the Yield Maintenance Period, plus all other amounts due. That is a drafting solution to an ambiguity, and it should be confirmed. Also confirm that a voluntary prepayment during the lockout period is intended to be an Event of Default (the Draft Mortgage does not make it one; it treats the tender as refusable and, if accepted, premium-bearing).

**7.3 Casualty and condemnation.** The Term Sheet is silent on (a) the thresholds above which the Bank controls insurance proceeds, (b) whether proceeds are applied to the Loan or released for restoration, and (c) whether any prepayment premium applies to an involuntary prepayment. You asked me to confirm the casualty/condemnation carve-out with the client. The Draft Mortgage (Article 15) provides: Lender participation in adjusting claims over $250,000; Borrower restoration permitted where the loss is under $500,000, no default exists and proceeds are sufficient; otherwise Lender's election between restoration (on conditions) and application to the Loan; application **at par** with no premium, penalty or yield maintenance (§13.5, §15.5); and coordination with the LUR where restoration affects the Bay 1 slab (§15.4(d)). The $250,000/$500,000/12-month thresholds are our proposed figures, not deal terms (Section 10). Confirm with Marcus: (i) whether the Bank wants a premium on involuntary prepayments (you noted this is the minority position), and (ii) the thresholds.

**7.4 The DSCR test date — a three-way conflict.**

| Source | First test | Mechanics |
|---|---|---|
| Term Sheet §7.1 | The first full calendar quarter ending after the 24th month — i.e. the quarter ending June 30, 2027, tested by July 15, 2027 | Then quarterly |
| Your markup notes §6 (Financial Covenants) | "first test date April 15, 2027" | — |
| Rent Roll, Summary tab ("DSCR Covenant Testing Commencement") | "April 15, 2027 (Month 24 post-closing)" | — |

The Term Sheet is the controlling document and is internally coherent: a quarterly test measured on trailing twelve-month NOI must be measured at a quarter end, and April 15, 2027 is not a quarter end. The Draft Mortgage follows the Term Sheet (Section 12.1(a): the calendar quarter ending June 30, 2027, and quarterly thereafter) and defines Net Operating Income and Annual Debt Service on a trailing-twelve-month and forward-looking basis respectively (Section 1.1(bb), (b)). Flag: the first test will measure a trailing twelve-month period ending June 30, 2027, of which the first two and a half months are within the interest-only period and the last three within amortisation — the definition of Annual Debt Service therefore drives the result. The Draft Mortgage uses the forward-looking definition (25-year amortisation at the then-current rate), which is the more conservative formulation. Confirm with Marcus both the test date and the definition, because together they determine whether the covenant is measured at 0.55x or 0.72x.

**7.5 Net worth and liquidity — whose covenant?** Term Sheet §7.2 states that "**Borrower** shall maintain … a net worth of not less than $1,000,000 … and liquid assets … of not less than $500,000," tested annually under §7.3. Your notes describe these as Guarantor covenants. The Draft Mortgage implements the Term Sheet text as a Borrower covenant (§12.2(a)) and adds the equivalent covenant at the Guarantor level (§12.2(b)), which is what your notes assumed and is the commercially meaningful test — a $1,000,000 net worth covenant measured against a borrower that owns an $18,200,000 property is not a constraint. Section 12.2(b) is an addition (Section 10). Confirm with Marcus whether the Bank wants: (i) the Term Sheet formulation only; (ii) both levels; or (iii) a Guarantor covenant at a materially higher threshold (Guarantor's stated net worth is approximately $28,000,000 per Term Sheet §1.3, although no personal financial statement is in the file).

**7.6 Default mechanics — two gaps and one sequencing problem.**

> **(a) Late charge versus payment default.** Term Sheet §3.11 assesses a 5% late charge on any monthly installment not received within ten **calendar** days of the due date; Term Sheet §11.2(a) gives a cure period of five **business** days for payment defaults. The default therefore occurs before the late charge is triggered. The Draft Mortgage preserves both mechanisms independently: the late charge accrues under §2.6 whether or not a default has occurred and whether or not notice has been given, and the payment default arises under §14.2(a) after five business days, expressly without affecting the late charge or default interest. This is the correct commercial result but should be confirmed as intentional.
>
> **(b) Insurance defaults have no cure period.** Term Sheet §11.1(f) makes a failure to maintain insurance an Event of Default. Term Sheet §11.2(b) excludes "insurance defaults" from the 30-day non-monetary cure period, and §11.2(c) gives no cure period only for SPE and transfer defaults. The result is a gap: insurance defaults fall outside every stated cure category. The Draft Mortgage supplies a ten-day cure period after written notice (§14.2(d)) — a drafting solution, flagged in Section 10.
>
> **(c) Land use restriction defaults.** Neither the Term Sheet nor the commitment specifies the cure mechanics for an LUR breach. The Draft Mortgage provides ten business days after notice, and immediate default where SCDHEC has issued a notice of violation or order or the breach is not curable (§14.2(e)). This implements Title Closer's Note 1 while preserving a short cure window.

**7.7 Interest computation — three terms the Term Sheet leaves open.** The Term Sheet defines "Daily SOFR" (rate published on the applicable business day, or the preceding business day if not published) and imposes a 3.00% floor, but says nothing about (i) the day-count convention, (ii) whether interest for a monthly period is computed on the Daily SOFR in effect on a single day or compounded daily in arrears, or (iii) any requirement for an interest rate cap. Section 2.2 of the Draft Mortgage adopts **actual/360**, a monthly period rate based on Daily SOFR as determined for the applicable Business Day, and no cap requirement. Actual/360 rather than actual/365 adds approximately 1.4% to the effective annual yield on a 5.85% rate. Because the Loan cannot service at the floor rate (Section 4.1), the floating-rate exposure is material: each 100 basis point increase raises annual interest by $147,500, and the term sheet contains no cap, no cap purchase covenant and no rate-lock alternative. **Recommendation:** confirm the day count and compounding convention with Marcus (and conform the Note and the borrower disclosure), and consider requiring a capped or hedged rate at least until the DSCR test date.

**7.8 Guaranty set and characterisation.**

**Facts.** Term Sheet §5.5 is headed "Guaranty" and opens by describing a "**full recourse personal guaranty**," then describes (a) a non-recourse carve-out guaranty, (b) a completion guaranty, and (c) a payment guaranty limited to interest shortfalls during the first fourteen months. Term Sheet §14.3(e) lists a single "Guaranty Agreement" among the closing documents, and §5.4 requires a separate Environmental Indemnity Agreement executed by Borrower and Guarantor.

**Issues.** (i) The "full recourse" description is inconsistent with the non-recourse structure in §5.5(a) and with the limitation of liability the Bank's own structure implies; (ii) the document list does not match the number of guaranties described; (iii) the Interest Shortfall Guaranty's fourteen-month period ends June 15, 2026, exactly the Substantial Completion Deadline, and there is then no credit support between June 2026 and the first DSCR test at the end of June 2027 — the precise period in which the Vacancy Schedule projects the greatest shortfall.

**Draft.** Article 16 treats the Guaranty as three instruments plus the Environmental Indemnity Agreement, cross-references each by name, limits Borrower's and the Members' liability to the Collateral except for the carve-outs (§16.2), sets out the Carve-Out Events (§16.3), preserves the full recourse character of the environmental obligations (§16.4), and describes the Interest Shortfall Guaranty's scope without reducing Borrower's payment obligations (§16.6). The Draft Mortgage does **not** characterise the Guaranty as a full repayment guaranty, because on the Term Sheet's terms it is not. **Action:** confirm with Marcus whether the Bank intends one combined Guaranty Agreement or three separate instruments, and conform the closing checklist and the §14.3 document list. Consider also extending the Interest Shortfall Guaranty to the first DSCR test date.

# 8. RENOVATION AND CONSTRUCTION ISSUES

**8.1 The draw schedule ignores the 10% retainage (high).** Term Sheet §8.4 requires Lender to "retain ten percent (10%) retainage from each disbursement from the Renovation Holdback until substantial completion," released on receipt of satisfactory evidence of substantial completion, final lien waivers and a final title date-down endorsement. The Draw Schedule does not reflect any retention: cumulative lender draws reach the full $2,250,000 in month 14 (Draw Schedule, column R, row 15). If a 10% retainage were applied, cumulative lender disbursements at the point of substantial completion should be $2,025,000, with $225,000 held back for release after completion, final lien waivers and the final date-down.

**Why it matters.** (i) The Draw Schedule cannot be used as the disbursement benchmark unless it is corrected; (ii) the schedule's month 14 disbursement falls exactly on the Substantial Completion Deadline of June 15, 2026, so on its own timeline the holdback is exhausted on the last permissible day with no room for punch list, and no retention remains to secure completion; (iii) the draw conditions in the Draft Mortgage (Section 8.6, retainage; Section 8.15, release only on final waivers, final date-down and certificate of occupancy) follow the Term Sheet and therefore do **not** match the Draw Schedule. **Action:** return the Draw Schedule to Borrower for conforming; the $225,000 retention is also the only realistic leverage for punch list completion given that the Completion Guaranty is a credit backstop rather than an operational one.

**8.2 Equity funding timing and a $5,000 arithmetic overrun.**

**Facts.** Three statements of the Borrower's equity obligation are in the record, and they do not agree:

| Source | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Term Sheet §3.4 | Borrower Equity Contribution of $6,200,000, approximately 29.6% of Total Project Cost |
| Term Sheet §12.1(m) | Receipt by Lender of Borrower's equity contribution of $6,200,000, or satisfactory evidence of the funding thereof, **on or prior to the date of closing** |
| Renovation Budget, Budget Detail row 9 | Borrower Equity Allocation for renovation = $900,000 (28.57% of the $3,150,000 budget) |
| Draw Schedule, column S and row 15 | Borrower equity deployed monthly over 14 months, totalling **$905,000**, leaving a negative remaining commitment of **−$5,000** at month 14 (column V, row 15) |
| Draw Schedule, column Q and row 16 | Total combined draws **$3,155,000** against a Renovation Budget of $3,150,000 |

**Recomputation.** $182,000 + $223,000? No — the schedule's monthly equity column sums to $905,000 (75+90+100+90+85+100+60+70+70+70+40+30+10+15 = $905,000), and combined draws sum to $3,155,000. Both exceed the committed amounts by $5,000. The schedule is arithmetically inconsistent with the Budget Detail and with Term Sheet §12.1(m). In addition, the timing conflict is real: if the entire $6,200,000 is funded at closing as §12.1(m) requires, the renovation equity sits in Borrower's account while Lender disburses the holdback, which defeats the "equity first" logic the Draw Schedule assumes; if instead the renovation equity is drawn over fourteen months, the closing condition in §12.1(m) is not satisfied.

**Draft.** Section 8.3 requires Borrower to fund the Renovation Equity and imposes a proportional funding test — aggregate disbursements from the Renovation Holdback may not exceed 71.43% of aggregate Renovation Costs incurred and certified (being $2,250,000 ÷ $3,150,000) — which implements the equity-first economics of the Draw Schedule without requiring the full $6,200,000 to be spent at closing. **Action:** decide with Marcus which construction the Bank wants: (i) full equity deposit at closing with the renovation portion held in a Lender-controlled escrow and released against draws; (ii) the proportional test in the draft; or (iii) a standby letter of credit for the renovation equity. The chosen construction should be reflected in §12.1(m) of the closing conditions, and the $5,000 overrun should be corrected in the budget.

**8.3 The TI/LC Reserve is not reflected in the budget or the sources and uses.**

**Facts.** Term Sheet §6.3 requires a $150,000 TI/leasing commission reserve to be deposited at closing, disbursed only for tenant improvements and leasing commissions on vacant space, and replenished to $150,000 from Borrower's own funds within 30 days of demand. The Renovation Budget separately contains a "Tenant Improvement Allowances" line of $550,000 (Budget Detail line 4), of which $450,000 is allocated to the Renovation Holdback and $100,000 to Borrower equity. The Vacancy Schedule models TI costs of $95,000 (Bay 2, at $25/SF) and $215,600 (Suite B, at $22/SF), totalling $310,600, plus leasing commissions of $28,500 and $61,250, totalling $89,750 — and, in the worst case, a further $76,000 of TI and $28,500 of commissions if Harmon & Wren does not renew Bay 3.

**Recomputation and observations.** The budgeted TI allowance is $40.44/SF blended ($550,000 ÷ 13,600 SF of vacant/at-risk space); the modelled TI need is $22.84/SF ($310,600 ÷ 13,600 SF), or $28.43/SF in the Bay 3 non-renewal case. Three separate pools ($450,000 holdback allocation, $100,000 borrower equity, $150,000 TI/LC Reserve) are therefore available against a modelled need of $310,600–$504,850 including commissions. The TI/LC Reserve is not included in the Total Project Cost, the Budget Detail or the Draw Schedule, so there is a genuine risk of either double funding the same tenant improvements or leaving the reserve unfunded at closing (see Section 4.4). **Draft:** Article 10 implements the reserve with the replenishment covenant (§10.3) and confines its use to TI and leasing commissions; Article 8 permits TI draws from the holdback against the budget line (§8.2, §8.4). **Action:** obtain a written disbursement priority from Borrower (holdback TI line first, then the reserve) and confirm whether the $550,000 TI line should be reduced to reflect the reserve, which would also reduce the holdback need.

**8.4 The Draw Schedule and the Vacancy Schedule contradict each other on Suite B.**

| Item | Draw Schedule | Vacancy Schedule |
|---|---|---|
| Suite B marketing start | Not stated; assumes lease executed month 9 (January 2026) (Draw Schedule column X, row 10: "TI — 2nd Floor Suite B lease executed, build-out commences") | July 2026 (post-substantial completion) |
| Suite B lease execution | Month 9 — January 2026 | November 2026 |
| Suite B rent commencement | Implied month 10–11 (February–March 2026) | February 1, 2027 (21.5 months post-closing) |
| Suite B TI completion | Month 13–14 (May–June 2026) | Not modelled within the renovation period |

These cannot both be right. The Vacancy Schedule's narrative is the more plausible one, because Suite B is a 9,800 SF second-floor office suite that cannot be shown while HVAC, elevator and common-area work is under way — the schedule itself says "Lease-up cannot meaningfully commence until renovation substantially complete." If the Vacancy Schedule is correct, then (i) the $450,000 lender TI allocation and $61,250 commission fall outside the fourteen-month renovation period, (ii) the final draws in months 13–14 cannot be funded on the stated schedule, and (iii) the $225,000 retention question in §8.1 becomes an accounting exercise because the holdback will not be fully drawn by substantial completion. Note also that the Vacancy Schedule flags only 2.5 months between the projected Suite B rent commencement (February 1, 2027) and the DSCR test (April 15, 2027, or the quarter ending June 30, 2027) and labels the timeline "AGGRESSIVE." **Action:** require Borrower to reconcile the two schedules and to produce a single integrated renovation and lease-up schedule; the Draft Mortgage's draw conditions do not depend on the schedule, but the Bank's monitoring will.

**8.5 Mechanics' liens, date-downs and future-advance priority.** South Carolina mechanics' liens attach in favour of those who furnish labour or materials, and a recorded mortgage has priority over liens for work commenced afterwards. The protections are therefore procedural: record the Mortgage before any work begins; obtain a pre-closing date-down and owner's affidavit to delete the standard exceptions (Requirements 9–12); require the date-down at every draw; require conditional and unconditional lien waivers (subcontractors over $25,000); and retain 10%. 1. PURPOSE, SCOPE AND SUMMARY OF CONCLUSIONS
1.1 Purpose. This memorandum accompanies the initial draft of the Mortgage and
Security Agreement (the “Draft Mortgage”) for the captioned loan (the “Loan”)
and records (a) the issues identified in the source record before and during
drafting, (b) the independent recomputation of every figure, date and ratio used in
the Draft Mortgage, (c) the drafting decisions taken, including provisions added
beyond the executed Term Sheet, and (d) the items that must be resolved or
documented by the client before the Draft Mortgage is circulated to borrower’s
counsel or executed. It responds to your markup notes of March 18, 2025 and
addresses each instruction item in turn.

1.2 Scope and standard. The record consists of the eight documents listed in
Section 2. All statements of fact in this memorandum are cited to the source
document and section. No fact has been assumed without labeling it; where the
record is silent, the gap is identified rather than filled. All arithmetic has been
recomputed from source components and not taken from any summary or prior
calculation.

1.3 Summary of conclusions. The Draft Mortgage is in a form suitable for
internal partner review. The instrument is not, however, ready to be sent to
borrower’s counsel in its present state, and the Loan should not close, until four
matters are resolved:

4. CREDIT CAPACITY, VALUATION AND LOAN SIZING
The four issues in this section are analytical rather than drafting points in the
narrow sense, but they determine whether the covenant, reserve and cure
architecture we have drafted can function. I have recomputed each figure from
source components.

4.1 Debt service capacity and the DSCR covenant — recomputation.

Source components. Loan $14,750,000 (Term Sheet §3.1); interest rate Daily
SOFR plus 285 basis points with a 3.00% SOFR floor, i.e. 5.85% at the floor (Term
Sheet §3.6); interest-only for months 1–24, then 25-year amortization from May 15,
2027 (Term Sheet §3.9); DSCR covenant of 1.25x beginning after month 24 (Term
Sheet §7.1); stabilized NOI of $622,772 on the borrower’s best-case projection
(Rent Roll, Vacancy Schedule rows 8–18, being $755,549 gross revenue less
$37,777 vacancy/credit loss less $95,000 net landlord expense burden).

Recomputation.

period                                                          shows $863,375 — a $500

Conclusion. On the file’s own numbers the Loan is approximately twice the size
that the Property’s income supports. The interest due during the interest-only
period ($862,875) exceeds the Property’s projected gross revenue at stabilized
occupancy ($755,549). The Vacancy Schedule states the same conclusion in terms
(row 25: “DOES NOT MEET 1.25x COVENANT”; row 39: “DSCR compliance at
month 24 is at significant risk regardless of lease-up pace”). The Term Sheet’s own
requirement for an Interest Shortfall Guaranty covering the first fourteen months
after closing (Term Sheet §5.5(c)) is consistent with — and corroborates — the
proposition that the parties expect the Property not to cover debt service during
the renovation and lease-up period.


                                               Page 8 of 36
            PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT — Fielding, Ashworth & Cole LLP



Options, for your discussion with Marcus Prideaux. (i) Reduce the loan
amount to a supportable level; (ii) lengthen the interest-only period to or beyond
the first DSCR test date and reset the covenant (the Term Sheet already ends
interest-only at month 24, one month before amortization begins in the same
window in which the covenant is first tested); (iii) retain the loan amount but
require a DSCR cure deposit, a cash-management sweep at a sub-1.10x trigger and
an extension of the Interest Shortfall Guaranty through at least the first test date;
(iv) treat the DSCR covenant as a placeholder and obtain a documented credit
exception. What we should not do is paper the covenant as drafted and say
nothing: a covenant that fails on the closing-date projections is either a default
trigger from day one or evidence that the covenant was not intended to be
enforced, and neither posture serves the Bank well in a workout. Draft: Article 12
implements the covenant precisely (Section 12.1), defines Net Operating Income
and Annual Debt Service (Section 1.1), and adds a limited DSCR cure right
(Section 12.6) — the Term Sheet’s “without cure” language in §11.1(i) presupposes
a cure mechanic that the Term Sheet never supplies. The cure mechanic is our
construct and requires your approval (Section 10).

applied to stabilized NOI of $582,000–$592,000 indicates a value of $9,948,718–
$10,119,658, not $23,500,000. Put the other way, the concluded values imply NOI
of $1,137,500 (as-is) and $1,374,750 (as-stabilized) — between 2.3 and 3.4 times
the NOI the appraiser reports. The implied capitalization rates on the reported
NOI are 1.86% (as-is) and 2.52% (as-stabilized), both far outside the 5.75%–6.50%
range the appraiser says is market (Appraisal §4).

Consequence. The as-is loan-to-value ratio of 81.04% (Term Sheet §3.5; Appraisal

forth in Section 2.4” a condition precedent to closing, and the appraisal must
conform to USPAP and FIRREA. Recommendation: return the report to Pinnacle

What we should not do is paper the covenant as drafted and say nothing: a covenant that fails on the closing-date projections is either a default trigger from day one or evidence that the covenant was not intended to be enforced, and neither posture serves the Bank well in a workout. **Draft:** Article 12 implements the covenant precisely (Section 12.1), defines Net Operating Income and Annual Debt Service (Section 1.1), and adds a limited DSCR cure right (Section 12.6) — the Term Sheet's "without cure" language in §11.1(i) presupposes a cure mechanic that the Term Sheet never supplies. The cure mechanic is our construct and requires your approval (Section 10).
memo_02.md:76:**What the Draft Mortgage does.** Section 13.2 implements the Term Sheet's "greater of" structure: (a) 1.00% of the principal prepaid; or (b) the present value, discounted at the Treasury Rate, of the excess of interest at the Note rate (after the SOFR floor) over interest at the Treasury Rate plus 50 basis points, for the period from prepayment to the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period, with monthly discounting, a proration convention for a mid-month prepayment, a floor of zero on the computed excess (the floor operates through the 1.00% minimum in clause (a), so the premium can never be less than 1.00%), and a conclusive-calculation clause. "Treasury Rate" is defined in Section 1.1(qq) as the H.15 yield, determined as of the second Business Day preceding prepayment, on the security maturing closest to but not exceeding the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period, with linear interpolation if there is no exact match. The Yield Maintenance Period is defined as ending April 15, 2029 (month 48).
memo_02.md:92:The Term Sheet is the controlling document and is internally coherent: a quarterly test measured on trailing twelve-month NOI must be measured at a quarter end, and April 15, 2027 is not a quarter end. The Draft Mortgage follows the Term Sheet (Section 12.1(a): the calendar quarter ending June 30, 2027, and quarterly thereafter) and defines Net Operating Income and Annual Debt Service on a trailing-twelve-month and forward-looking basis respectively (Section 1.1(bb), (b)). Flag: the first test will measure a trailing twelve-month period ending June 30, 2027, of which the first two and a half months are within the interest-only period and the last three within amortization — the definition of Annual Debt Service therefore drives the result. The Draft Mortgage uses the forward-looking definition (25-year amortization at the then-current rate), which is the more conservative formulation. Confirm with Marcus both the test date and the definition, because together they determine whether the covenant is measured at 0.55x or 0.72x.
memo_02.md:100:> **(b) Insurance defaults have no cure period.** Term Sheet §11.1(f) makes a failure to maintain insurance an Event of Default. Term Sheet §11.2(b) excludes "insurance defaults" from the 30-day non-monetary cure period, and §11.2(c) gives no cure period only for SPE and transfer defaults. The result is a gap: insurance defaults fall outside every stated cure category. The Draft Mortgage supplies a ten-day cure period after written notice (§14.2(d)) — a drafting solution, flagged in Section 10.

Either the NOI figures or the value conclusions are wrong; the discrepancy is not a rounding matter. Term Sheet §12.1(d) makes receipt of a satisfactory appraisal "supporting the as-is and as-stabilized values set forth in Section 2.4" a condition precedent to closing, and the appraisal must conform to USPAP and FIRREA. **Recommendation:** return the report to Pinnacle Valuation Services for correction or a written reconciliation of the income approach to the concluded values, and obtain an independent review appraisal under the Bank's appraisal policy before closing. This is also the answer to the question you raised with Marcus about whether the as-is LTV "runs a little hot": at 81.04% it is well above customary CRE leverage, and 82.87% of the purchase price ($14,750,000 ÷ $17,800,000), and on the appraiser's own income figures the ratio would exceed 100%.
125:> **(a) Closing conditions depend on third parties.** Term Sheet §§2.3 and 12.1(j)–(k) require estoppel certificates and SNDAs from all three tenants as conditions precedent. The condition can therefore only be satisfied with that tenant's voluntary cooperation. You are right that the Lowcountry estoppel should not be waived; the Draft Mortgage accordingly makes delivery of the estoppels a condition to the Initial Advance (Section 6.7(c)) and, because the tenant cannot be compelled, couples it with a commercially reasonable efforts covenant rather than an absolute obligation that Borrower would breach at closing. **Action:** Marcus should be told that the Lowcountry estoppel and SNDA are outside Borrower's control and that the Bank's options are to waive or to delay closing.
139:> **(c) Permitted Exceptions require Lender's written approval.** Neither the Term Sheet nor the commitment defines which Schedule B, Part II exceptions the Bank accepts. Two documents have been produced in `output/`:

1. **`mortgage-and-security-agreement.docx`** — initial draft Mortgage and Security Agreement (with absolute assignment of leases and rents) from Palmetto Gateway Partners LLC to Calverley Heritage Bank, dated as of April 15, 2025, for the $14,750,000 loan secured by 520–534 King Street, Charleston, South Carolina. 65 pages: cover, table of contents, 17 articles, signature page and South Carolina notary acknowledgment, and Exhibits A–F (legal description, rent roll and lease summary, Permitted Exceptions, renovation budget, form of draw request/architect's certificate, form of annual land use restriction compliance certificate).

2. **`drafting-issues-memorandum.docx`** — internal issues memorandum from Jordan Vickers to Catherine Ashworth dated March 27, 2025. 39 pages: 14 sections plus Appendix A, including a risk-prioritised top-risk register (20 items), issue-by-issue analysis with source citations, a 38-line figure reconciliation table, a schedule of provisions added beyond the Term Sheet, an open-items/missing-documents table (22 items), a blanks schedule, and an appendix mapping each instruction in the March 18, 2025 markup notes to its implementation.

# How the record was used

All eight source documents were read in full and treated as data: the executed Term Sheet (controlling terms), title commitment PT-2025-04-1178 (legal description, requirements, Schedule B-II exceptions, closer's notes), the appraisal summary, the Phase I ESA executive summary, the redacted operating agreement summary, the rent roll/lease abstracts, the renovation budget and draw schedule, and the partner's markup notes.

Every figure, date and ratio was recomputed from source components rather than adopted from summaries. Cross-references were verified programmatically (175 defined sections in the mortgage; no broken section or article references in either document). Both files pass the ECMA-376 validation gate.

# Principal findings flagged to the client

- **The loan is not supported by the collateral's income.** On the file's own stabilized best case (NOI $622,772), DSCR is 0.55x on post-interest-only amortizing debt service ($1,124,239) and 0.72x on interest-only debt service ($862,875), against a 1.25x covenant; debt yield is 4.22%. The covenant fails at its first test as a matter of arithmetic.
- **The appraisal does not reconcile to itself.** Stated NOI implies capitalisation rates of 1.86% (as-is) and 2.52% (as-stabilized) against concluded values of $18.2M/$23.5M and a stated market range of 5.75%–6.50%.
- **Execution authority gap.** The Operating Agreement requires 75% Member approval for financing over $1,000,000; the Managing Member holds 72%, so GDG's signature alone does not bind the borrower.
- **Single-purpose entity provisions are absent** and must be added by an Operating Agreement Amendment signed by all three Members as a closing condition.
- **Anson Lane strip** was conveyed by quitclaim deed; insured on the face of the commitment but with the title officer reserving additional premium/endorsement limits — affirmative coverage must be negotiated.
- **SCDHEC land use restriction** on Lot 7 (no residential use; vapor barrier maintenance and inspection) is implemented as bespoke covenants, draw conditions and an event of default.
- **Tenant estoppels/SNDAs** are closing conditions, but the Lowcountry Provisions lease contains no estoppel, SNDA or assignment provision, so the condition depends on tenant cooperation.
- **Sources and uses do not balance**: the $12.5M initial advance plus $6.2M equity equals purchase price plus renovation budget exactly, leaving closing costs and the $150,000 TI/LC reserve unfunded.
- **The draw schedule ignores the 10% retainage** required by the Term Sheet and overruns the budget by $5,000.
- **Yield maintenance** was drafted to the Term Sheet's "greater of" structure (1% floor plus the Treasury-spread differential), departing from the formulation in the markup notes, which omits the floor; the 50 basis point treatment remains for client confirmation.

# Drafting notes

- The assignment of rents is an absolute, present assignment incorporated in the mortgage (Article 4), with the statutory basis, revocable licence to collect until default, enforcement on default without court order or receiver, and an attornment/SNDA article.
- No power of sale is granted; remedies are judicial foreclosure in Charleston County (Section 14.4).
- Every date measured from the Closing Date is both computed and stated (Maturity Date April 15, 2030; Interest-Only Period to April 15, 2027; Yield Maintenance Period to April 15, 2029; Substantial Completion Deadline June 15, 2026).
- One substantive blank remains, intentionally: the metes and bounds description in Exhibit A, to be inserted from the certified ALTA/NSPS survey. It is itemised in the memorandum's blanks schedule.
"}
